rationale: A wins because it treats the missing facts as gates, not garnish: “a policy or category reporter will not run a story on an unnamed asset” is exactly the discipline this update needs. B has some real shapes, but “Correspondent banks are Wise's real target as £30B stablecoin bet lands” abuses the £30B figure and turns total Wise volume into implied stablecoin exposure. That is not seasoning; that is a fact problem wearing a headline.
gaps_in_A: “the first-market decision is the news” leans on a first-market fact the update never supplies; the set later asks for it, but the angle should be explicitly conditional.
“A listed, profitable payments company is now settling business transfers in stablecoin” slightly overstates a launch with no named stablecoin, partner, customer, or disclosed stablecoin volume.

“Wise tells business customers correspondent banking is the slow lane” is a sharp conflict frame, but without a measured corridor, amount, time, and fee delta it risks laundering Wise’s marketing claim into a story.
gaps_in_B: “£30B stablecoin bet” misuses Wise’s total quarterly cross-border volume as if it were stablecoin volume or exposure. That is the kind of overclaim reporters punish.
“EU MiCA, U.S. stablecoin bills, UK FCA regime, Asian frameworks” imports regulatory specifics not supplied in the update. Useful questions, yes; fake-ready context, no.
“Visa, Stripe, PayPal, Mastercard” appear as comparable moves without evidence in the supplied facts. Proof requirements should not quietly smuggle in an assumed trend.
“Customer story — hallucinated_fact” throws out a valid second-wave angle. A customer story is not fabricated if it is clearly gated on a named customer, corridor, amount, and result.
